'''''Crataegus laevigata''''', known as the '''Midland hawthorn''',<ref name="GRIN">{{GRIN | accessdate = 1 January 2018}}</ref> '''English hawthorn''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''woodland hawthorn''',<ref name=GRIN/> or '''mayflower''', is a species of [[Crataegus|hawthorn]] native to western and central Europe, from [[Great Britain]] (where it is typically found in [[ancient woodland]] and old hedgerows<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20220115122419/https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/crataegus-laevigata ''Online Atlas of the British and Irish Flora'': ''Crataegus laevigata'']</ref>) and [[Spain]], east to [[Romania]] and [[Ukraine]]. The species name is sometimes spelt ''C. levigata'',<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gutermann, W. |year=2011 |title=Notulae nomenclaturales 41-45. (New names in ''Cruciata'', ''Kali'', and some small corrections) |journal=Phyton: Annales Rei Botanicae |volume=51 |issue=1 |pages=95–102}}</ref> but the original orthography is  ''C. lævigata''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Poiret, J.L.M. |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/15262 |title=Encyclopédie Méthodique. Botanique |publisher=H. Agasse |year=1798 |editor-last=J.B.A.P.d.M. De Lamarck |volume=4 |location=Paris |pages=437–447 |chapter=Néflier; Mespilus}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Christensen, K.I. |last2=Talent, N. |year=2013 |title=''Crataegus laevigata'' or ''C levigata'' – a Paleographic Analysis |journal=Phyton: Annales Rei Botanicae |volume=52 |issue=2 |pages=195–201}}</ref>

==Description==
It is a large [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] growing to {{Convert|8|m|ft|abbr=on}} or rarely to {{Convert|12|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, with a dense crown. The [[leaf|leaves]] are {{Convert|2–6|cm|in|sigfig=2|abbr=on}} long and {{Convert|2–5|cm|in|sigfig=2|abbr=on}} broad, with two or three shallow, forward-pointing lobes on each side of the leaf. The [[plant sexuality|hermaphrodite]] [[flower]]s are produced in [[corymb]]s of 6 to 12, each flower with five white or pale pink petals and two or sometimes three styles.  They are pollinated by [[insect]]s. The [[fruit]] is a dark red [[pome]] {{Convert|6–10|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} diameter, slightly broader than long, containing two or three [[Pyrena|nutlets]].{{cn|date=September 2024}}
[[File:Aubépine épineuse. Crataegus laevigata. Mahieddine Boumendjel.jpg|thumb|''Crataegus laevigata'' (fruits)]]

It flowers in May to June (UK) in rather lax clusters. The flowers are usually white, but can be pink. Flowers are up to 2.4 cm in diameter, with 2–3 styles and stigmas and more than 20 stamens. They have 5 triangular sepals, which are obtuse. The petals can be slightly velvety on the inside.<ref name=Collins>{{cite book |last1=Streeter |first1=David |title= Collins Wild Flower Guide |date=2019 |publisher=HarperCollins |location=London|isbn=978-0-00-815674-9}}</ref>

Its fruit [[persistence (botany)|persists]] for an average of 64.4 days, and bears an average of 2.8 seeds per fruit. Fruits average 77.4% water, and their [[dry matter|dry weight]] includes 11.1% [[carbohydrate]]s and 1.4% [[lipid]]s.{{sfn|Ehrlén|Eriksson|1991}}

The Midland hawthorn is distinguished from the closely related common hawthorn, ''[[Crataegus monogyna|C. monogyna]]'', in the leaves being only shallowly lobed, with forward-pointing lobes, without hair tufts in the vein axils, and in the flowers having more than one style.  Each style produces a seed, so its fruits also have more than one seed and these make them slightly oval, in contrast with the single-seeded and therefore round fruits of common hawthorn. The two species [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridise]], giving rise to [[Crataegus × media|''C.'' × ''media'']].{{cn|date=September 2024}}

==Taxonomy==
In the past, Midland hawthorn was widely but incorrectly known by the name ''[[Crataegus oxyacantha|C. oxyacantha]]'', a name that has now been rejected as being of uncertain application. In 1753, [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] introduced the name ''C. oxyacantha'' for the single species of which he was aware, but described it in such a way that the name became used for various species, including both the Midland and the common hawthorn. In 1775, [[Nicholaas Jacquin|Jacquin]] formally separated the common hawthorn, naming it ''C. monogyna'',<ref>Jacquin, N.J. 1775. Florae Austriacae sive Plantarum Selectarum in Austriæ archiducatu: sponte crescentium icones, ad vivum coloratæ, et descriptionibus, ac synonymis illustratæ.</ref> and in 1946, [[James Edgar Dandy|Dandy]] showed that Linnaeus had actually observed a different plant,  ''C. oxyacantha''. By this time, though, confusion over the true identity of ''C. oxyacantha'' was so great that [[Jean Irene Byatt|Byatt]] proposed<ref>Byatt, J. (1974). ''Bot. J. Linn. Soc.'' 69: 15–20.</ref> that the name should be formally rejected as ambiguous, and this proposal was accepted by the [[International Botanical Congress]],<ref>Brummitt, R. K. (1986). ''Taxon'' 35: 556–563.</ref> although the name continues to be used informally.

The Midland hawthorn was described botanically as a separate species as long ago as 1798 by [[Jean Louis Marie Poiret|Poiret]], whose name ''Mespilus laevigata'' referred to this hawthorn. Poiret's name is reflected in the revised formal botanical name of Midland hawthorn: ''Crataegus laevigata'' (Poir.) DC.{{cn|date=September 2024}}

==Cultivars==
'François Rigaud' has yellow fruit.<ref name="Phipps">Phipps, J.B.; O'Kennon, R.J.; Lance, R.W. 2003. ''Hawthorns and medlars''. Royal Horticultural Society, Cambridge, U.K.</ref>

'Paul's Scarlet'<ref>{{Cite web |title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Crataegus laevigata'' 'Paul's Scarlet' |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/93812/Crataegus-laevigata-Paul-s-Scarlet-(d)/Details |access-date=15 April 2020}}</ref> (double red flowers), 'Punicea'<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Crataegus laevigata'' 'Punicea' |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/49409/Crataegus-laevigata-Punicea/Details |access-date=5 May 2020 |publisher=RHS}}</ref> (pink and white) and 'Rosea Flore Pleno'<ref>{{Cite web |title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Crataegus laevigata'' 'Rosea Flore Pleno' |url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=572 |access-date=20 July 2013}}</ref> (double pink flowers) have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]. These cultivars are considered by taxonomists to be derived from hybrids between ''C. laevigata'' and ''C. monogyna'', within the named hybrid species ''C.'' × ''media''.<ref name=Phipps/>

==Parasites==
The hawthorn button-top gall on Midland hawthorn is caused by the dipteran gall-midge ''[[Dasineura crataegi]]''.{{cn|date=September 2024}}
